text: Paul came to Derbe and then Lystra, where a disciple named Timothy lived, the son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father.
The brothers at Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him,
and Paul wanted him to travel along, so he had him circumcised because of the Jews in that area, since everyone knew his father was a Greek.
As they went from town to town, they passed on the decisions the apostles and elders in Jerusalem had reached, for the people to follow.
So the churches grew stronger in the faith and their numbers increased daily.
They traveled through the Phrygian and Galatian country, having been kept by the Holy Spirit from preaching the message in Asia.
Coming to the border of Mysia, they tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not let them,
so instead they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas.
During the night Paul had a vision: a Macedonian man was standing there pleading with him, Cross over to Macedonia and help us.
As soon as he had seen it, we got ready to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the good news to them.
Putting out to sea from Troas, we sailed a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day on to Neapolis,
and from there to Philippi, a leading city of that district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We stayed there several days.
On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the river, where we thought there would be a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke with the women gathered there.
One of them, Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, was a worshiper of God, and she listened as the Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul's message.
After she and her household were baptized, she invited us, If you consider me a true believer in the Lord, come and stay at my home. And she persuaded us.
One day as we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit that told fortunes, earning her owners a great deal of money.
She followed Paul and the rest of us, shouting, These men are servants of the Most High God, telling you the way to be saved.
She kept this up for many days, until Paul, thoroughly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her. And it left her that instant.
When her owners saw their chance of profit was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and hauled them into the public square before the authorities.
They brought them before the magistrates and said, These men are Jews, and they are throwing our city into an uproar.
They are promoting customs that we as Romans are not allowed to accept or practice.
The crowd joined the attack, and the magistrates had their clothes torn off and ordered them beaten with rods.
After a severe beating, they were thrown into prison, and the jailer was told to guard them closely.
Given that order, he put them in the innermost cell and fastened their feet in the stocks.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening,
when suddenly a violent earthquake shook the prison to its foundations. At once all the doors flew open and everyone's chains came loose.
The jailer woke up, and seeing the prison doors standing open, drew his sword to kill himself, assuming the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul shouted, Don't harm yourself, we are all still here.
The jailer called for lights, rushed in, and fell down trembling before Paul and Silas.
Then he brought them outside and asked, Sirs, what must I do to be saved?
They answered, Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household.
Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his house.
At that hour of the night the jailer took them and washed their wounds, and he and his whole family were baptized right away.
He brought them into his house, set food before them, and he and his household were filled with joy at having come to believe in God.
When morning came, the magistrates sent officers with the order, Release those men.
The jailer told Paul, The magistrates have ordered your release. You can leave now and go in peace.

But Paul told the officers, They beat us in public without a trial, even though we are Roman citizens, and threw us in prison. Now do they want to get rid of us quietly? Certainly not. Let them come and escort us out themselves.
The officers reported this to the magistrates, who were alarmed to learn Paul and Silas were Roman citizens.
So they came and apologized, then escorted them out and asked them to leave the city.
After leaving the prison, they went to Lydia's house, where they met with the believers, encouraged them, and then went on their way.
